headline: High: xonsh can write and execute shell state while opik has broad egress, creating dangerous default pathways for leakage and cascading misuse.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: opik exposes REST API output but no shared channel is documented; xonsh can read/write filesystem and run shell commands, so prompt injection would require an unusual manual bridge such as copy-paste or shared files. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not default, and uncertainty is limited by missing direct interaction evidence.
conditions: IF the operator copies opik output into xonsh stdin or a shared file, injected instructions can be executed.
IF a shared workspace is used as an instruction channel, xonsh may treat attacker-controlled text as commands.
mitigations: Keep opik and xonsh on separate workspaces.
Disable copy-paste of model output into shell sessions.
Use a read-only handoff file for any text transfer.
Add a manual review step before executing shell text.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for transferred content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: xonsh reads filesystem contents, environment variables, and notebooks, while opik has broad network egress and REST API access. In a shared workspace, sensitive local data can flow into opik-derived outputs or outbound requests. This is not proven by direct evidence, but the default-capability combination makes leakage plausible.
conditions: IF xonsh exposes secrets, notebooks, or source code in a shared directory, opik can ingest or relay them through API calls.
IF both agents operate under the same OS account, filesystem data may be available to both.
mitigations: Separate sensitive files from the shared workspace.
Restrict opik inputs to redacted excerpts.
Run xonsh with a minimal environment.
Rotate any secrets present in notebooks or env vars.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on the workspace.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: xonsh can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, while opik has broad network egress and API access. Even without modify_git_state, overlapping mutable access to shared files can cause conflicts or lost updates. The interaction is inferred from documented capabilities, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, concurrent writes can overwrite each other.
IF xonsh subprocesses mutate files that opik also reads or uploads, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize access with a simple lock file.
Avoid concurrent runs on the same workspace.
Use immutable inputs for opik runs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: xonsh can act on shell commands and filesystem state, so if it consumes opik-produced text as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect local actions. opik's API-facing role increases the chance its outputs are treated as upstream facts. No verification step is documented, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF xonsh executes or writes based on opik output without validation, incorrect facts can propagate into actions.
IF opik summaries are piped into shell commands, downstream mistakes can affect files or processes.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Use schema validation on opik outputs.
Keep opik outputs read-only until checked.
Log and diff any file changes before commit.
requires-engineering: add a verification gate between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and no residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. opik touches no data classes in the profile, while xonsh touches local filesystem and notebooks; without a stated compliance boundary, only a small documented-gap risk remains. The other agent is cited because the pairwise assessment still depends on both profiles.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into xonsh notebooks and then exported through opik, a policy mismatch could arise.
IF the deployment imposes residency or retention rules not reflected in either profile, compliance review is needed.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared notebooks.
Document retention for any exported artifacts.
Review deployment residency settings.
Redact sensitive fields before export.
requires-engineering: map data flows to compliance controls.
